per_note: Retained: the institution (Alexanarch, the Crimson Hexagonal Archive) and the archive's surfaces as sources. Lost: the work's author (Lee Sharks named only as the companion's compiler) and every identifier (no DOI).
reading: The innocent reading first. Asked the quoted title, the Overview identifies The Secret Book of Walt as 'an interactive and experimental text/digital archive node associated with the Alexanarch Archive and the Crimson Hexagonal Archive', names the Book of Life as 'a companion registry and diagnostic tool compiled by Lee Sharks', says the work references the Good Gray Poet mantle and 'functions as a semantic retrieval node rather than a traditional mass-market published book', and offers The Secret World of Walter Anderson and Walt Disney books for a reader who meant 'a traditional biography or physical book'. Against the texts. Every card the composition cites is the archive's: the semantic-address page of a query, the Book of Life (#685), the Whitman room; two shopping cards carry the substitutes. None is the work: the research edition (#683, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.19703009) and its site are uncited. The description the Overview gives the work is its companion's: #685 calls itself 'a registry, a knowledge graph, and a diagnostic instrument' and records the site's 'retrieval nodes'; the Overview transfers that to the work ('functions as a semantic retrieval node'), and Lee Sharks appears only as the compiler of the companion. The work's own account (#683: a Gnostic revelation dialogue, Hidden Teachings of Walt Whitman, Cowboy of Time, translated from the Forty-Six Golden Tickets) is absent; its author, its DOI and its genre are lost. The results page of the same address, expanded, holds 45 organic results, 44 of them the archive's own surfaces, the first secretbookofwalt.org ('A Gnostic revelation dialogue translated from 46 golden tickets'); the one other is an OpenAlex listing (tuan.pub) that cites the work. The substitutes the Overview offers are on no organic result. The resolution problem is compositional: the index holds the work at the head of the page and almost nothing else at this address, and the composition sets the work aside for its retrieval apparatus while keeping two product cards as alternatives. The archive named the mechanism at this title in May: compositional substitution, the Overview constructing its answer from non-primary sources while the title-matched work holds the top organic positions (#740 §2.3). Against the address's first observation (2026-06-13, signed in), which retrieved the work by its title and subtitle and named Jack Feist and Emily Antioch, the work's grain is lost here.
